 China’s 2027 Registered Capital Deadline: Should You Pay In, Scale Down, or Restructure?
 11 November 2026 
 Posted by China Briefing 
 Written by
 Giulia Interesse 
 In this article 
 China’s 30 June 2027 registered capital deadline requires many existing foreign-invested companies to adjust their capital contribution schedules under the revised Company Law. We explain the requirements, compliance risks, and strategic options for businesses considering whether to retain, reduce, or restructure their registered capital. 
 Foreign-invested companies registered in China on or before 30 June 2024 have until 30 June 2027 to align their capital contribution schedules with the revised Company Law. For most limited liability companies, including wholly foreign-owned enterprises (WFOEs), that means amending the articles of association so that any unpaid registered capital is due by 30 June 2032 at the latest.
 Many investors set registered capital years ago on lengthy contribution schedules, treating it as a signal of commitment rather than an obligation that would need to be funded in the near term. Before the deadline, each must decide whether that capital is money the business will actually need.
 This article explains what the rules require, what is at stake, and how to choose between the options.
 China’s 2027 registered capital deadline: What foreign investors need to do
 Under the  revised Company Law , in force since 1 July 2024, shareholders of a limited liability company must pay their subscribed capital in full within five years of establishment.  State Council Decree No. 784 applies the rule to existing companies through a three-year transition period:
 Limited liability companies: Limited liability companies whose remaining contribution period runs more than five years beyond 1 July 2027 must shorten it so that all capital is due by 30 June 2032 and record the change in their articles by 30 June 2027.
 Joint stock companies: Promoters must  pay their subscribed shares in full by 30 June 2027.
 Abnormal figures: Registration authorities may require companies to adjust registered capital amounts or contribution periods that are “obviously abnormal”, taking into account factors such as business scope, actual operations, asset size, and the shareholders’ capacity to contribute.
 Disclosure: changes to subscribed or paid-in capital must be published on the National Enterprise Credit Information Publicity System within 20 working days.
 For limited liability companies,  30 June 2027 is the deadline for fixing the schedule, not for paying the money . The decision on how much capital to keep, however, must be made now.

 Get the resolutions and amended articles for your new contribution schedule drafted, and your company registration updated.

 What happens if a company misses the deadline?
 A company that fails to adjust is first ordered to correct its schedule; if it still does not comply, it is publicly flagged on the national credit system (Decree No. 784, Article 6), where banks and counterparties will see it.
 The larger risk sits in the  Company Law itself , which now treats unpaid capital as a live liability:
 The board must verify contributions and issue written calls for overdue capital; directors who fail to do so are liable for resulting losses (Article 51);
 A shareholder who still does not pay after a grace period of at least 60 days can lose the corresponding equity (Article 52); or
 If the company cannot pay its debts as they fall due, the company or its creditors can demand unpaid capital ahead of schedule (Article 54).
 Unpaid registered capital is no longer merely a registration figure. It is a legally enforceable contribution obligation that directors may need to pursue, and creditors may be able to accelerate under certain circumstances.
 Should you pay in, scale down, or restructure?
 Before reducing registered capital, companies should also assess whether the existing amount remains necessary for commercial or regulatory reasons. Although China no longer imposes general minimum capital requirements, banks, major customers, government procurement authorities, and sector-specific regulators may still view registered capital as an indicator of financial strength. A significant reduction may therefore affect financing, bidding, or commercial negotiations.
 Keep the capital and set a realistic schedule
 This makes sense where the capital matches a real investment plan or where a licence, tender, or banking relationship depends on it. The task is then to set a timetable the parent can fund and plan the foreign exchange steps for each injection.
 Reduce registered capital
 Reducing capital suits companies whose figure was set for appearances. It is a  formal process : a shareholder resolution passed by at least two-thirds of voting rights, a balance sheet and asset list, written notice to creditors within 10 days, and a public announcement within 30 days. Creditors then have 30 days from notice, or 45 days from the announcement, to demand repayment or security, and reductions must be proportional unless all shareholders agree otherwise.
 Cutting unpaid capital returns no cash; reducing paid-in capital to send funds abroad also requires bank registration and a tax analysis. With the creditor process alone taking up to 45 days, companies that wait until mid-2027 risk running out of time.
 Restructure
 For groups with several Chinese entities, the deadline also prompts merging or closing dormant companies rather than funding them. Two rules matter here. The revised Company Law expressly allows equity and  creditor-right contributions in a broader range of circumstances. As a result, shareholder loans already advanced may, in some cases, be converted into registered capital, subject to appraisal, corporate approvals, and foreign exchange requirements. But selling equity does not shed the obligation: a seller remains secondarily liable if the buyer fails to pay the outstanding capital.
 FAQs
 Do foreign-invested companies in China have to pay registered capital within five years?
 Yes. For limited liability companies established on or after 1 July 2024, subscribed capital generally must be paid within five years of establishment. Existing companies benefit from transitional arrangements and must adjust their contribution schedules by 30 June 2027, with any remaining capital generally due by 30 June 2032.
 Is 30 June 2027 the deadline to pay in registered capital?
 Not for limited liability companies: for them, it is the deadline to amend the contribution schedule. Promoters of joint stock companies, however, must pay in full by then.
 Can a WFOE reduce its registered capital?
 Yes, through a formal capital reduction with creditor notice, a public announcement, and registration with the market regulator. The creditor process alone can take up to 45 days.
 What happens if a company does not adjust its capital schedule in time?
 The registration authority will order it to correct the schedule and, if it fails to do so, flag the company publicly on the National Enterprise Credit Information Publicity System.
